lead: LPI's entry-level security certificate. It covers the security basics every computer user and new IT member should know: risk and ethics, encryption, device and data protection, network safety, and identity and privacy. One short exam, no prerequisites, and it never expires.
objSub: Five topics and 16 objectives from LPI's Security Essentials (020-100) objectives. Tick objectives as you study; your progress stays on this device.

v10.label: Version 1.0
v10.note: The only version. No prerequisites. LPI weights each objective; the 16 objectives add up to 40, the same as the number of questions. Delivered at Pearson VUE test centers or online with OnVUE.
v10.onote: Objective titles and numbers from LPI's 020-100 objectives. LPI weights objectives out of 40; the bars show each topic's share of that total.

domains.name: Security Concepts
obj: Goals, Roles and Actors
Weight 1. Why IT security matters; confidentiality, integrity, availability and non-repudiation; who attacks and why.
Risk Assessment and Management
Weight 2. Where to find security information, classifying incidents and vulnerabilities, assessments, forensics, ISMS and incident response.
Ethical Behavior
Weight 2. How your security actions affect others, handling vulnerabilities and confidential data responsibly, and the legal side of scans and attacks.

domains.name: Encryption
obj: Cryptography and Public Key Infrastructure
Weight 3. Symmetric, asymmetric and hybrid encryption, hashing, key exchange, perfect forward secrecy, PKI, CAs, X.509 certificates and revocation.
Web Encryption
Weight 2. HTTPS and TLS, how certificates tie to websites, and reading the browser's security messages.
Email Encryption
Weight 2. OpenPGP and S/MIME, key servers, and sending signed and encrypted email.
Data Storage Encryption
Weight 2. File, container and full-disk encryption with tools like VeraCrypt and BitLocker, and encrypting cloud files with Cryptomator.

domains.name: Device and Storage Security
obj: Hardware Security
Weight 2. Computer parts, IoT and smart devices, physical access risks, USB, Bluetooth and RFID, and trusted computing.
Application Security
Weight 2. Getting software from safe sources, keeping firmware, OS and apps updated, app stores, common software flaws and protective software.
Malware
Weight 3. Malware types, rootkits and remote access, scanners, spyware and data theft.
Data Availability
Weight 2. Backups (full, differential, incremental), storing them safely, and the risks of cloud storage, sharing and sync.

domains.name: Network and Service Security
obj: Networks, Network Services and the Internet
Weight 4. Network media and devices, IP and routing, MAC and IP addresses, ports, DNS, key protocols, and IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Network and Internet Security
Weight 3. Link-layer access, Wi-Fi security (WEP, WPA, WPA2), interception, man-in-the-middle, DoS, botnets and packet filtering.
Network Encryption and Anonymity
Weight 3. VPNs, end-to-end vs transport encryption, proxies, Tor, the darknet and how addresses identify you.

domains.name: Identity and Privacy
obj: Identity and Authentication
Weight 3. Digital identity, AAA, strong passwords, password managers, MFA and one-time codes, SSO, account recovery and password attacks.
Information Confidentiality and Secure Communication
Weight 2. Data leaks and interception, phishing and social engineering, spam, attachments, secure sharing and encrypted messaging.
Privacy Protection
Weight 2. The value of personal data, tracking with cookies and fingerprinting, social media privacy settings and data rights like GDPR.

extras.title: Encryption in one card
rows: Fast. Used for bulk data, like AES. The hard part is sharing the key safely.
Public key encrypts or checks, private key decrypts or signs. Slower.
Asymmetric swaps a symmetric key, which then encrypts the data. How TLS works.
A fixed-size fingerprint. Proves data didn't change; can't be reversed.
Proves who sent it and that it wasn't altered.

extras.title: Backup types
rows: Fast to make; a restore needs the full plus every incremental.
A restore needs the full plus the latest differential.
Deletes and ransomware sync too. Keep separate copies.

extras.title: Spot a phishing message
rows: Check the real sender address, not just the display name.
Hover over links before clicking: does the domain match the sender?
Watch for urgency, threats or rewards that push you to act fast.
Don't open unexpected attachments, especially macros or archives.
When in doubt, contact the sender through a channel you already trust, and report the message.

method: Use the 16 objectives as your checklist. Network and Service Security and Encryption carry the most weight.
LPI's free learning materials follow the objectives one to one. Read one lesson a day.
Turn on MFA everywhere you can, set up a password manager, and encrypt a USB drive with VeraCrypt. Real use makes it stick.
Flashcards for encryption types, backup types, Wi-Fi standards and common attacks.
Take a timed practice set of 40 questions in 60 minutes before you book.
tips: Many questions turn on one term: authentication vs authorization, encryption vs hashing, backup vs sync.
The focus is protecting yourself and your data, not running enterprise tools.
Scanning or attacking systems without permission is illegal. Expect questions on it.
There's no penalty for guessing, so always answer.

quiz.q: An attacker changes the amount on a wire transfer while it's in transit. Which security goal was violated?
o: Integrity
Right. Integrity means data isn't changed without authorization.
Confidentiality
Confidentiality is about who can read the data. Here it was altered.
Availability
The system and data stayed available.
Non-repudiation
Non-repudiation stops a sender from denying they sent something.

quiz.q: You find a serious bug in a vendor's software. What's the most ethical next step?
o: Report it privately to the vendor and give them time to fix it (responsible disclosure)
Right. Users stay protected while the fix is made.
Post the exploit online right away
That arms attackers before anyone can patch.
Use it to look around other people's systems
That's illegal access.
Sell it to the highest bidder
That puts users at risk and may be illegal.

quiz.q: Which statement about hashing is true?
o: A hash is one-way: you can't get the original data back from it
Right. Hashes prove integrity and store passwords; they aren't meant to be decrypted.
A hash can be decrypted with the right key
That's encryption, not hashing.
Changing one character leaves the hash the same
Even a tiny change produces a completely different hash.
Hashes are always longer than the input
Hashes are a fixed size, whatever the input length.

quiz.q: Your browser warns that a site's certificate was issued to a different domain. What does this mean?
o: The certificate doesn't match the site, so the connection may not be who it claims to be
Right. Don't enter credentials; it could be misconfigured or an interception.
The site is faster than usual
Certificates don't affect speed.
Your password is expired
Unrelated to certificates.
The site uses strong encryption, so it's safe
Encryption to the wrong party isn't safe.

quiz.q: You want to send an email that the recipient can verify came from you and wasn't changed. What do you use?
o: A digital signature with OpenPGP or S/MIME
Right. Signing with your private key proves origin and integrity.
Bcc
Bcc hides recipients. It proves nothing.
A larger font
Formatting has nothing to do with authenticity.
Compressing the message
Compression doesn't prove who sent it.

quiz.q: A laptop holding personnel records is stolen. Which control MOST protects the data?
o: Full-disk encryption, like BitLocker
Right. Without the key, the drive is unreadable.
A strong screen saver password
Someone can pull the drive and read it in another machine.
Antivirus
It doesn't protect data on a stolen drive.
Daily backups
Backups help you recover the data, not keep it from the thief.

quiz.q: You find a USB stick in the parking lot. What should you do?
o: Don't plug it in; turn it in to IT or security
Right. Dropped USB drives are a classic way to deliver malware.
Plug it in to find the owner
That's exactly what the attacker hopes for.
Format it and keep it
Plugging it in to format it is already the risk.
Give it to a coworker to check
That just moves the risk to them.

quiz.q: Ransomware encrypted a laptop, and the encrypted files synced to the cloud folder too. What would have saved the data?
o: Separate, versioned backups that sync can't overwrite
Right. Sync copies changes, including bad ones. Backups keep older versions.
A faster internet connection
Speed doesn't protect data.
More cloud storage space
The problem was copying the damage, not space.
Turning off the screen saver
Unrelated.

quiz.q: Why is public Wi-Fi at an airport risky?
o: Others on the network may intercept traffic or run a fake access point
Right. Use HTTPS and a trusted VPN on networks you don't control.
It uses too much battery
Not a security issue.
It blocks all websites
It usually doesn't.
It's always WPA3, so it's safe
Open networks often have no encryption at all, and a fake hotspot can claim any name.

quiz.q: Thousands of infected home devices flood a website with traffic until it goes down. What is this?
o: A DDoS attack using a botnet
Right. Many compromised devices attacking at once is a distributed denial of service.
Phishing
Phishing tricks people with messages.
SQL injection
That targets a database through input fields.
Man-in-the-middle
That intercepts traffic between two parties.

quiz.q: What does a VPN mainly protect?
o: Your traffic between your device and the VPN server, from people on the local network
Right. Past the VPN server, traffic is only as private as the site and the provider allow.
Everything you do, making you completely anonymous
The VPN provider and the sites you log in to can still identify you.
Your device from malware
A VPN isn't antivirus.
Your passwords from being weak
It doesn't fix weak passwords.

quiz.q: Which is an example of multi-factor authentication?
o: A password plus a code from an authenticator app
Right. Something you know plus something you have.
A password plus a security question
Both are things you know: still one factor type.
Two different passwords
Same factor type twice.
A longer password
Still one factor.

quiz.q: A website tracks you across other sites even after you clear cookies, using details like your screen size, fonts and browser version. What is this?
o: Browser fingerprinting
Right. A combination of device details can identify you without cookies.
Encryption
Encryption protects data; it doesn't track you.
A firewall
Firewalls filter traffic.
Two-factor authentication
2FA is about logging in.

pbqs.title: Name the threat
pbqs.scenario: Six situations a user reported. Pick the threat each one shows. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.log:
From: IT-Helpdesk <support@it-heIpdesk.example>
Your mailbox is full. Log in within 1 hour to avoid losing email:
http://it-heIpdesk.example/login
items.why: A look-alike domain, urgency and a login link: phishing.

items.log:
All your files have been encrypted.
Send 0.5 BTC to restore them. 48 hours remaining.
items.why: Encrypted files and a ransom demand: ransomware.

items.log:
CoffeeShop_Guest   (open)
CoffeeShop_Guest   (open)  <- two with the same name
CoffeeShop-Staff   (WPA2)
items.why: A second network copying the real name is likely a fake hotspot.

items.log:
Successful sign-in to your shopping account from a new device.
You reused this password on a site that was breached last month.
items.why: Leaked username and password pairs reused on another site: credential stuffing.

items.log:
An app you didn't install is using the microphone and location in the background
and sending data to an unknown server.
items.why: Secretly collecting and sending your data: spyware.

items.log:
Your connection is not private
The certificate is issued to: free-wifi-portal.example
items.why: A certificate for the wrong site on your bank's page points to someone in the middle.

pbqs.title: Protect the data
pbqs.scenario: For each need, pick the BEST control and what it mainly protects. Some options aren't used.

rows.req: A lost laptop must not expose its files
rows.why: Encryption keeps the data unreadable without the key.
Separate, versioned backups bring the data back.

rows.req: Use a unique, strong password for every site
rows.why: A password manager makes unique passwords practical.

rows.req: A stolen password alone shouldn't be enough to log in
rows.why: MFA adds a second factor the thief doesn't have.

rows.req: Hide your traffic from others on hotel Wi-Fi
rows.why: A trusted VPN encrypts traffic on the local network.

rows.req: Close known holes attackers use to get in
rows.why: Patches fix flaws that let attackers change or run code on your system.
